[PATH:empirical] Psychophysical experiments using continuous flash suppression (CFS) or binocular rivalry with ramped versus abrupt stimulus onset, measuring subjective reports of awareness. — Directly tests whether subjective experience correlates with rate of change (rapid onset) rather than static magnitude (steady stimulus) under unimodal visual conditions.

[PATH:theoretical] Computational modeling of neural adaptation and contrast gain control in primary sensory cortex (e.g., V1) to predict perceived intensity from temporal derivatives of input. — Provides mechanistic framework linking rate of change to qualia, allowing quantitative predictions that can be compared to empirical data.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing fMRI/EEG studies on temporal dynamics of sensory perception (e.g., studies on transient versus sustained neural responses and their correlation with subjective ratings). — Synthesizes available evidence on whether neural markers of subjective experience align more with derivative or magnitude of sensory signals, identifying gaps or support for the hypothesis.

C006.subject: subjective experience (qualia)
C006.object: the dynamic interaction of multisensory integration and cognitive processes
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: subjective experience (qualia) the dynamic interaction of multisensory integration and cognitive processes]

[PATH:empirical] Neuroimaging studies comparing multisensory integration (e.g., audiovisual binding) with subjective reports of unified conscious experience in tasks like the McGurk effect or rubber hand illusion — Directly tests whether variations in multisensory integration strength correlate with changes in qualia reports, providing causal or correlational evidence for the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental paradigms manipulating cognitive load (e.g., working memory or attention) while measuring multisensory integration and subjective experience ratings — Allows dissociation of cognitive process contributions from purely sensory integration, helping to confirm or refute the claim that dynamic interaction is primary.

[PATH:theoretical] Review of predictive processing and Bayesian brain models linking multisensory integration to conscious perception — Provides a formal framework to derive testable predictions about qualia emergence from the interaction of sensory and cognitive systems, and to evaluate explanatory coherence against competing theories.

qualifier.geographic: global, with emphasis on Western research institutions

C007.object: visual and auditory signals are desynchronized beyond a 150-ms window, even when spatial cues are congruent
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: subjective experience (qualia) visual and auditory signals are desynchronized beyond a 150-ms window, even when spatial cues are congruent]

[PATH:empirical] A controlled psychophysical experiment using audiovisual stimuli with millisecond-precision asynchrony (e.g., 0–300 ms) and congruent spatial cues, measuring subjective temporal binding judgments and self-reported qualia coherence via continuous scales. — Directly tests the 150-ms disruption threshold under spatial congruence, providing quantitative data on subjective experience disruption.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of existing literature on temporal binding windows in multisensory integration, focusing on studies that manipulated audiovisual asynchrony while controlling spatial congruence. — Aggregates prior evidence to assess consistency of the 150-ms threshold across paradigms and populations, identifying potential confounds or moderators.

[PATH:theoretical] Computational model of cross-modal perception (e.g., Bayesian causal inference or neural oscillation framework) that simulates qualia disruption as a function of asynchrony and spatial congruence, predicting subjective breakpoints. — Provides mechanistic predictions that can be compared to empirical data, helping to refine or refute the hypothesized threshold and its dependence on spatial cues.

C008.subject: subjective experience (qualia)
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: subjective experience (qualia) neural architecture and processing mechanisms]

[PATH:empirical] Neurophenomenological experiments using first-person reports (e.g., G. Tononi's integrated information theory, IIT) combined with fMRI or MEG to correlate specific qualia (e.g., color, pain) with precise neural activity patterns in the posterior cortical hot zone — Directly tests the causal link between neural architecture and subjective experience by manipulating neural states (e.g., via TMS or psychedelics) and measuring changes in reported qualia, potentially confirming or refuting the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative neuroanatomy studies across species (e.g., humans vs. cephalopods) to identify necessary and sufficient neural correlates of consciousness (NCC) by examining convergent evolution of complex qualia — If qualitatively similar subjective experiences arise from vastly different neural architectures, it would refute the hypothesis that qualia are primarily determined by specific human neural mechanisms; if not, it would support the architecture-specific claim.

[PATH:theoretical] Computational modeling of recurrent neural networks trained on sensory tasks (e.g., deep neural networks for object recognition) to test whether internal representations exhibit qualia-like properties (e.g., integrated information or causal structure) — Provides a formal test of whether processing mechanisms alone (without biological wetware) can generate subjective experience, thereby isolating the role of architecture from other factors like embodiment or biological chemistry.

C009.subject: subjective experience (qualia)
C009.object: temporal synchrony when attention is divided, but by static magnitude when attention is focused
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: subjective experience (qualia) temporal synchrony when attention is divided, but by static magnitude when attention is focused]

[PATH:empirical] Dual-task psychophysical experiments measuring temporal order judgments (TOJ) and intensity judgments under divided vs. focused attention conditions — Directly tests whether divided attention biases subjective experience toward temporal synchrony (e.g., judging cross-modal stimuli as simultaneous) while focused attention biases toward static magnitude (e.g., judging stimulus intensity). Comparing TOJ thresholds and magnitude estimation across attention conditions can confirm or refute the hypothesized dominance shift.

[PATH:empirical] Neuroimaging studies (fMRI or EEG) examining attentional modulation of multisensory integration areas (e.g., superior temporal sulcus, intraparietal sulcus) during divided vs. focused attention — If temporal synchrony dominates under divided attention, neural activity should show enhanced phase-locking or cross-modal binding in temporal processing regions; if static magnitude dominates under focused attention, activity should shift to regions encoding intensity or salience. Such neural correlates can provide converging evidence for the hypothesized attentional modulation of qualia.

C010.subject: subjective experience (qualia)
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: subjective experience (qualia) static magnitude and temporal synchrony]

[PATH:empirical] Direct replication of early 21st century cross-modal attentional paradigms (e.g., Shimojo & Shams, 2001; Spence, 2010) with concurrent first-person reports of qualia strength and objective measures of temporal synchrony judgments. — Systematically manipulating the magnitude (e.g., intensity of auditory/visual stimuli) and temporal synchrony (e.g., stimulus onset asynchrony) while collecting subjective reports of qualia (e.g., perceived vividness, unity) can directly test whether these physical parameters are independent of the subjective experience.

[PATH:theoretical] Computational modeling of Bayesian causal inference in multisensory perception (e.g., Körding et al., 2007) extended to predict subjective qualia ratings vs. objective synchrony thresholds. — If subjective experience is independent of static magnitude and temporal synchrony, Bayesian models that optimally combine sensory cues based on these parameters should fail to predict subjective reports. Contrasting model predictions with empirical data can reveal dissociations.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of published studies on multisensory integration and attention (e.g., Talsma et al., 2010; Macaluso & Driver, 2005) focusing on correlations between physical synchrony/magnitude and subjective reports of unity or presence. — A systematic review can quantify the strength and consistency of the relationship across paradigms, identifying whether reported independence is an artifact of specific tasks or a robust phenomenon.
